sentences.text: The genus Martinectes is known from multiple skeletons and skulls, though it contains only a single species.
This large polycotylid plesiosaur measured at least around 5 meters in length.
It belongs to the class Reptilia.
Recent estimates suggest the animal weighed 1.27 metric tons.
Some researchers believe its size was similar to that of Polycotylus.
Two large specimens, catalogued as KUVP 40001 and 40002, were collected from the Pierre Shale of Wyoming.
Adams officially described these specimens as a new species of Trinacromerum in 1997.
Later, O'Keefe demonstrated that the specimen did not belong to Trinacromerum and assigned it to Dolichorhynchops.
Clark and colleagues found several characters distinguishing this animal from the type species of Dolichorhynchops.
Everhart suggested that specimen KUVP 40001 could have measured up to 6 to 7 meters in length.
The genus Martinectes was described by Clark, O'Keefe, and Slack in 2023.
The type species of the genus Martinectes is Trinacromerum bonneri.
Martinectes bonneri was previously known as Trinacromerum bonneri and Dolichorhynchops bonneri.
Clark, O'Keefe, and Slack classified Martinectes as a polycotylid member of the clade Leptocleidia.
Martinectes, along with Dolichorhynchops species, forms the clade Dolichorhynchia within the Polycotylinae.
Martinectes belongs to the family Polycotylidae.
Martinectes belongs to the subfamily Polycotylinae.
The parent group of Martinectes is the clade Dolichorhynchia.
Martinectes lived during the Late Cretaceous in North America and possibly European Russia.
The animal lived between 83.6 and 72.2 million years ago during the Campanian stage.

In 2023, Clark, O'Keefe, and Slack assigned Dolichorhynchops bonneri from the Sharon Springs Formation to the new genus Martinectes, meaning "Martin's swimmer". In 2025, polycotylid teeth from the Rybushka Formation of European Russia were referred to cf. Martinectes.
